fields.title: Judges
fields.subtitle: Shofetim, “Judges”
fields.description: The book of the generation that grew up “who did not know the LORD or what he had done for Israel”, and of the God who kept rescuing them anyway. Again and again Israel turns to other gods, falls under its enemies, cries out, and is saved by a deliverer God raises up: Othniel; left-handed Ehud; Deborah the prophet and Jael with her tent peg; Gideon, the least in his family, with three hundred men, torches and jars; Jephthah and his terrible vow; and Samson, set apart from the womb, who pulled down a temple at the last. Each time the rescue lasts only as long as the deliverer lives, and the book ends in civil war with its haunting refrain: “In those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did what they thought was right.” In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Hebrew given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the book’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the book of Judges about?
qa.answer: The history of Israel between the death of Joshua and the rise of the monarchy. It traces a repeated pattern, set out in chapter 2: the people turn to other gods, God gives them over to their enemies, they cry out, and God raises up a judge who rescues them, until the judge dies and the people fall back further than before. Its central chapters (3–16) tell the stories of twelve judges, and its last chapters (17–21) show how far Israel fell, under the refrain “In those days there was no king in Israel.”

qa.question: Who wrote the book of Judges, and when?
qa.answer: The book does not name its author. Jewish tradition assigned it to the prophet Samuel. Many scholars see it as part of a longer history running from Deuteronomy to Kings, drawing on older sources such as the Song of Deborah and completed later, perhaps around the time of the exile. Its refrain about there being no king suggests it was written, at least in its final form, after the monarchy had begun. The events it describes span the centuries between Joshua and Saul, though their exact dates are debated.

qa.question: Who were the judges of Israel?
qa.answer: Leaders God raised up to rescue Israel from its oppressors and to govern it afterward; the Hebrew word means more than a judge in a law court. The book names twelve: Othniel, Ehud, Shamgar, Deborah (with Barak), Gideon, Tola, Jair, Jephthah, Ibzan, Elon, Abdon and Samson. Six are given fuller accounts (the “major” judges) and six are mentioned only briefly. None was a king, and none founded a lasting line; Gideon’s son Abimelech, who made himself king, is the book’s picture of what bad rule looks like.

qa.question: Did Jephthah really sacrifice his daughter?
qa.answer: Readers have disagreed since ancient times. Jephthah vowed to offer as a burnt offering whatever came out of his house to meet him, and his only daughter came out first. The text says that after two months “he did to her what he had vowed” (11:39). Many, ancient and modern, take this to mean that he sacrificed her, a tragic sign of how far Israel had absorbed the religion of Canaan; others, noting the stress on her never marrying, read it as a lifelong dedication to the LORD’s service. Either way, the book does not approve the vow, and it records that Israel’s young women mourned her every year.

qa.question: Why is Samson in the Hall of Faith in Hebrews 11?
qa.answer: Hebrews 11:32 names Samson alongside Gideon, Barak, Jephthah, David and Samuel among those who “found strength when they were weak”. The letter does not praise his character, which Judges shows to be deeply flawed. It honours the moments when he trusted God, above all his last prayer in the Philistine temple: “Lord GOD, please remember me” (16:28). His inclusion, like the others’, shows that God works through weak and failing people who turn to him.

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. “LORD” in capitals stands for God’s personal name, and the Song of Deborah in chapter 5 is set out line by line as poetry. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Hebrew beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
Whenever the LORD raised up a judge for them, the LORD was with that judge and saved them from the power of their enemies as long as the judge lived. For the LORD was moved to pity when they groaned under those who oppressed and tormented them.

— Judges 2:18

Judges is the darkest book in the history of Israel, and one of the most honest books in the Bible. It begins where Joshua left off, with the land given and much of it still to be taken, and a people who have just promised, three times over, to serve the LORD. It ends, twenty-one chapters later, with a civil war, a tribe almost wiped out, and a sentence that sums up everything in between: “In those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did what they thought was right.”

Between those two ends are some of the most vivid stories ever written: a left-handed assassin, a woman with a tent peg, a farmer threshing wheat in a winepress, three hundred men with torches and jars, a strongman with seven braids. Children love these stories, and adults are often unsettled by them. Both reactions are right. Judges is a book about the mercy of God and the downward pull of the human heart, and it does not soften either.

Who were the judges?

The Hebrew name of the book, Shofetim, means “judges”, but the word means more than the English suggests. A few of these leaders settled disputes. Deborah held court under a palm tree, and the Israelites “came up to her to have their disputes decided.” But most of them are judges in an older sense: leaders raised up by God to set things right, to rescue his people from their oppressors and to govern them afterward. The book’s own summary makes that clear: “the LORD raised up judges, who rescued them from the power of those who plundered them.” The word it uses again and again for what they do is not “judge” but “save”.

There are twelve of them. Six are given fuller accounts (the “major” judges): Othniel, Ehud, Deborah with Barak, Gideon, Jephthah and Samson. Six more are named only briefly: Shamgar, Tola, Jair, Ibzan, Elon and Abdon. None of them is a king. They come from different tribes, at different times, often ruling only part of the land, and when each one dies, there is no one to take their place.

The shape of the book

  • Two openings (1:1–3:6). The first tells, tribe by tribe, how Israel failed to drive out the Canaanites. The second steps back to explain the pattern that will run through the whole book.
  • The stories of the judges (3:7–16:31). Twelve deliverers, from Othniel, the model judge, to Samson, the most gifted and the most wayward.
  • Two closing stories (chapters 17–21). A household shrine stolen by a whole tribe, and a crime in Gibeah that leads to civil war. Neither has a judge in it. Both are framed by the refrain “In those days there was no king in Israel.”

The two openings and the two endings mirror each other. At the start the tribes fight Canaanites together; at the end they fight one another. At the start a judge from Judah, Othniel, wins a wife by courage; at the end the tribes of Israel get wives for Benjamin by kidnapping. The book is not just a list of episodes. It is the story of a slide.

The cycle

The second opening, in chapter 2, explains it all in advance. It begins with one of the saddest sentences in the Bible:

That whole generation also died and was gathered to their ancestors, and after them another generation grew up who did not know the LORD or what he had done for Israel.

— Judges 2:10

Then it describes a pattern that the stories will repeat. The Israelites do what is evil in the sight of the LORD and serve the Baals. The LORD hands them over to their enemies. They cry out to him. He raises up a judge who rescues them, and the land has peace. Then the judge dies, and the people turn back to other gods, and it begins again.

Readers often call it a cycle, but the book itself says it is worse than that. When each judge died, the people “would turn back and behave worse than their ancestors.” It is a spiral, and it winds downward. The early judges are men and women of faith; the later ones are increasingly compromised; and by the last chapters the people of God are doing things the Canaanites were judged for.

What does not change, through all of it, is God. The verse at the head of this introduction gives the reason he keeps raising up deliverers: “the LORD was moved to pity when they groaned.” In chapter 10, after Israel has abandoned him yet again, he tells them to cry to the gods they chose for themselves. They put away those gods, and then comes one of the most tender lines in the Old Testament: “he could bear Israel’s misery no longer.” The mercy of God in Judges is not earned. It is the only reason the book does not end sooner.

Othniel and Ehud

The first judge is Othniel, Caleb’s younger brother (or, as some read it, his nephew), and his story is told in five verses, as a pattern for the rest: Israel sins, cries out, and “the LORD raised up a deliverer”. “The Spirit of the LORD came on him, and he judged Israel.” He wins, and “the land had peace for forty years.” There is nothing in his story to regret.

Then comes Ehud, and the book changes tone. He is from Benjamin, a name that means “son of the right hand”, and he is left-handed, which lets him carry a sword on his right thigh past the guards of Eglon, the very fat king of Moab. The story is told with dark humour, down to the servants waiting outside the locked door, thinking the king is relieving himself. God uses an unlikely man and an unexpected means, and the land has rest for eighty years.

Deborah, Barak and Jael

Chapters 4 and 5 tell the same victory twice, first in prose and then in one of the oldest poems in the Bible. Israel is oppressed by Jabin, king of Canaan, whose general Sisera has nine hundred iron chariots. Deborah, “a prophet” who “was judging Israel at that time”, summons Barak to lead the army. He will go only if she goes with him. She agrees, but tells him that “the LORD will hand Sisera over to a woman.”

The battle is won when the LORD throws Sisera’s army into panic, and the song tells how even the weather fought for Israel: “the stars, along their courses, made war on Sisera.” The woman who ends the war is not Deborah but Jael, the wife of a Kenite, who welcomes the fleeing Sisera into her tent and kills him as he sleeps. The song calls her “blessed above all women”, and then, with startling sympathy, imagines Sisera’s mother at her window, waiting for a son who will never come home.

Deborah is the only judge in the book described as a prophet, and the only one shown deciding cases. Christians read her leadership in different ways: some see in her a precedent for women leading God’s people, others an exception the book itself marks as unusual in a time of weak men. All can agree on how the song remembers her: “a mother in Israel.”

Gideon

Gideon is introduced hiding. He is threshing wheat in a winepress, down out of sight, so that the Midianite raiders will not take it. And the angel of the LORD greets him with words that sound almost like a joke: “The LORD is with you, mighty warrior.” Gideon’s answer is the honest question of every generation that has heard of God’s wonders but not seen them:

Gideon answered him, “Pardon me, my lord, but if the LORD is with us, why has all this come upon us? Where are all his wonders that our ancestors told us about when they said, ‘Did not the LORD bring us up from Egypt?’ Now the LORD has abandoned us and handed us over to Midian.”

— Judges 6:13

God does not answer the question. He gives a commission: “Go in this strength of yours… Am I not the one sending you?” And when Gideon protests that his clan is the weakest and he is the least in his family, God gives the only answer that matters: “I will be with you.” Gideon builds an altar and names it “The LORD Is Peace.”

The rest of the story is about God making sure the victory will be his. Gideon asks for signs, twice, with a fleece, and God patiently gives them. Then God reduces the army from thirty-two thousand to three hundred, so that Israel could never say, “Our own strength has saved us.” At night the three hundred surround the Midianite camp, break their jars, raise their torches, blow their horns and shout, “A sword for the LORD and for Gideon!” The enemy flees in confusion.

Afterwards the people ask Gideon to found a dynasty. His answer is the right one: “I will not rule over you, and my son will not rule over you. The LORD will rule over you.” But then he makes a golden ephod from the plunder, and “all Israel prostituted themselves by worshiping it, and it became a trap for Gideon and his family.” And he names one of his sons Abimelech, “my father is king”.

Abimelech and Jotham’s fable

Abimelech takes the name at its word. He murders seventy of his brothers on a single stone and has himself made king at Shechem. Only the youngest, Jotham, escapes, and from a mountaintop he tells the first fable in the Bible: the trees went looking for a king, and the olive, the fig and the vine all declined, too busy bearing fruit. Only the bramble accepted, offering the cedars its shade, or fire. Abimelech’s three-year reign ends with a woman dropping a millstone on his head. Israel’s first attempt at kingship is a bramble.

Jephthah

Jephthah is the son of a prostitute, driven out by his half-brothers, who becomes the leader of a band of outlaws. When the Ammonites attack, the elders of Gilead come begging. He is a good negotiator and a brave fighter, and “the Spirit of the LORD came on Jephthah.” But before the battle he makes a vow no one asked him to make: whatever comes out of his house to meet him when he returns in victory, he will offer as a burnt offering. The one who comes out, dancing with tambourines, is his only child, his daughter.

Readers have argued for centuries about what happened next. The text says that “he did to her what he had vowed”, and many, ancient and modern, take this to mean that he sacrificed her, in a terrible imitation of the Canaanite religion all around him. Others, noting that the passage dwells on her never marrying, have read it as a lifelong dedication to the LORD’s service. Either way, the story is a tragedy, and the book offers no word of approval. The daughter is remembered: “Every year the young women of Israel would go out for four days to commemorate the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite.”

Samson

The last judge has the most remarkable beginning. An angel announces his birth to a childless woman, in a pattern that runs from Sarah to Elizabeth, the mother of John the Baptist. He is to be a Nazirite from the womb, set apart to God, with no razor ever touching his head, and he “will begin to save Israel from the power of the Philistines.” When his father asks the angel’s name, the answer is, “Why do you ask about my name? It is wonderful.”

And yet Samson spends his life breaking almost everything he was set apart for. He goes after Philistine women, eats honey from a dead lion, makes riddles and loses his temper. The Spirit of the LORD rushes on him again and again, and he tears a lion apart with his bare hands and kills a thousand men with the jawbone of a donkey. But he never leads Israel into battle, and he never seems to pray except for himself. Finally Delilah coaxes the secret of his strength from him, his hair is cut, and the saddest words in his story follow: “But he did not know that the LORD had left him.”

Blind, shackled, grinding grain in a Gaza prison, Samson prays once more:

Then Samson called out to the LORD: “Lord GOD, please remember me. Please give me strength just this once more, O God, so that with one blow I may pay the Philistines back for my two eyes.”

— Judges 16:28

He pulls down the temple of Dagon, “he killed more people by his death than he had killed during his whole life.” It is a strange, mixed ending, part revenge and part faith. Samson only began to save Israel, as the angel said. The rescue would have to be finished by someone else.

The Spirit of the LORD

Judges speaks often of the Spirit of the LORD. The Spirit comes on Othniel and Jephthah; clothes Gideon like a garment; rushes on Samson. It is clear that God’s Spirit empowered these deliverers to do what they could not have done themselves. It is equally clear that the gift was not a reward for godliness, and that it did not make them godly. Gideon still made an idol, Jephthah still made his vow, Samson still went to Gaza. The book is a lasting warning not to mistake power for holiness.

When there was no king

The last five chapters have no judges at all. A man named Micah sets up a private shrine with an idol and hires a wandering Levite as his priest, saying, “Now I know that the LORD will treat me well, because I have a Levite as my priest.” Then the tribe of Dan, looking for land, steals the idol and the priest, massacres a peaceful town, and sets up their own sanctuary.

The last story is one of the most terrible in the Old Testament. A Levite’s concubine is abused to death by men of Gibeah, a town of Benjamin, in a scene that deliberately echoes Sodom. The Levite cuts up her body and sends it to the tribes. Israel goes to war against Benjamin and nearly destroys it, then, to save the tribe, kills the men of another town and seizes women for wives. The narrator offers no comment except the refrain. The horror is the comment.

The refrain points forward. Israel needs a king, a good one. The closing stories are full of names that will matter in the next book: a Levite from Bethlehem, a woman from Bethlehem, the town of Gibeah. Bethlehem will be David’s town; Gibeah will be the home of Saul.

How to read Judges

Read the book straight through, if you can, in two or three sittings, so that the slide is felt. Watch for the repeated phrases: “did what was evil in the sight of the LORD”, “cried out to the LORD”, “the Spirit of the LORD”, “the land had peace”. Notice that the refrain about peace disappears after Gideon. Notice who prays, and who does not.

The book does not name its author. Jewish tradition assigned it to Samuel; many scholars see it as part of a longer history from Deuteronomy to Kings, completed later, perhaps in the time of the exile. Its stories cover perhaps three centuries between Joshua and Saul, though the dates of the judges, some of whom may have overlapped in different regions, are much debated.

Above all, do not read Judges as a gallery of heroes to copy. The letter to the Hebrews does name Gideon, Barak, Samson and Jephthah among those who acted through faith, and it is right to: each, at some moment, trusted God. But the book is not about their virtue. It is about a God who kept rescuing a people who kept forgetting him, and who was preparing, through all their failure, to give them a better deliverer.

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and given freely to the public domain. It is printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. A few of its choices in Judges are worth knowing before you begin.

“The LORD.” Where the Hebrew uses God’s personal name, the four letters often written Yahweh, this translation follows long Jewish and Christian custom and writes “the LORD”. Where it uses the ordinary word for God, it writes “God”.

“A deliverer.” The Hebrew word for one who saves is translated “deliverer”, as when “the LORD raised up a deliverer for them” in Othniel’s and Ehud’s day.

The Spirit’s coming. The translation keeps the different verbs the Hebrew uses: the Spirit “came on” Othniel, “clothed” Gideon, and “rushed on” Samson.

“What they thought was right.” The book’s refrain, familiar from older Bibles as “every man did that which was right in his own eyes”, is rendered “everyone did what they thought was right.”

Poetry. The Song of Deborah in chapter 5 is printed one line per line, as the poetry it is.

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Hebrew beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: Judges 1
fields.body_html:
Judah goes up first

After Joshua died, the Israelites asked the LORD, “Which of us should go up first to fight against the Canaanites?” The LORD answered, “Judah is to go up. I have handed the land over to them.” Judah said to his brother Simeon, “Come up with me into the territory allotted to me, and let us fight the Canaanites together. Then I will go with you into your territory.” So Simeon went with them. When Judah went up, the LORD handed the Canaanites and the Perizzites over to them, and they defeated 10,000 men at Bezek. They came upon Adoni-Bezek at Bezek and fought against him, and they defeated the Canaanites and the Perizzites. Adoni-Bezek ran away, but they chased him and caught him, and they cut off his thumbs and his big toes. Adoni-Bezek said, “Seventy kings, their thumbs and big toes cut off, used to pick up scraps under my table. God has paid me back for what I did.” They brought him to Jerusalem, and he died there.

The men of Judah fought against Jerusalem and captured it. They struck it down with the sword and set the city on fire. After that the men of Judah went down to fight the Canaanites who lived in the hill country, the Negev and the foothills. Judah marched against the Canaanites who lived in Hebron, which used to be called Kiriath-arba, and they defeated Sheshai, Ahiman and Talmai. From there they went against the people who lived in Debir. Debir used to be called Kiriath-sepher. Caleb said, “I will give my daughter Achsah as a wife to the man who attacks Kiriath-sepher and captures it.” Othniel son of Kenaz, Caleb’s younger brother, captured it, so Caleb gave him his daughter Achsah as his wife. When she came to Othniel, she urged him to ask her father for a field. As she got down from her donkey, Caleb asked her, “What do you want?” She answered, “Give me a gift. You have given me land in the Negev; now give me springs of water too.” Caleb then gave her the upper springs and the lower springs.

The descendants of the Kenite, Moses’ father-in-law, went up with the people of Judah from the city of palm trees into the wilderness of Judah, in the Negev near Arad. They went and settled among the people. Then Judah went with his brother Simeon, and they defeated the Canaanites who lived in Zephath. They devoted the city to destruction, so it was named Hormah. Judah also captured Gaza, Ashkelon and Ekron, each with its surrounding territory. The LORD was with Judah, and they took the hill country for their own. But they could not drive out the people who lived on the plain, because those people had iron chariots. Hebron was given to Caleb, as Moses had promised, and he drove out the three sons of Anak from there. But the people of Benjamin did not drive out the Jebusites who lived in Jerusalem, and the Jebusites have lived there with the people of Benjamin to this day.

The house of Joseph takes Bethel

The house of Joseph also went up against Bethel, and the LORD was with them. The house of Joseph sent men to spy out Bethel, which used to be called Luz. The spies saw a man coming out of the city. “Please show us a way into the city,” they said to him, “and we will show you faithful love.” So he showed them the way in, and they struck the city down with the sword, but they let the man and his whole clan go free. The man went off to the land of the Hittites, where he built a city and named it Luz. That is still its name today.

Canaanites left in the land

But Manasseh did not drive out the people of Beth-shean, Taanach, Dor, Ibleam or Megiddo, or of the villages around them, because the Canaanites were determined to stay in that land. Later, when Israel had grown stronger, they made the Canaanites do forced labor, but they never drove them out completely.

Ephraim did not drive out the Canaanites who lived in Gezer, so the Canaanites went on living among them there.

Zebulun did not drive out the people living in Kitron or in Nahalol, so the Canaanites lived among them, though they were made to do forced labor.

Asher did not drive out the people living in Acco or Sidon, or in Ahlab, Achzib, Helbah, Aphik or Rehob. So the Asherites lived among the Canaanites who lived in the land, because they did not drive them out.

Naphtali did not drive out the people living in Beth-shemesh or Beth-anath, but lived among the Canaanites who lived in the land. The people of Beth-shemesh and Beth-anath were made to do forced labor for them.

The Amorites forced the people of Dan back into the hill country and would not let them come down into the plain. The Amorites were determined to stay in Mount Heres, Aijalon and Shaalbim, but the house of Joseph pressed hard on them, and they were made to do forced labor. The border of the Amorites ran from the Ascent of Akrabbim, from Sela and on up.

fields.title: Judges 2
fields.body_html:
The angel of the LORD at Bochim

The angel of the LORD went up from Gilgal to Bochim. He said, “I brought you up from Egypt, and I brought you into the land I had promised on oath to your ancestors. I said, ‘I will never break my covenant with you, and you must make no covenant with the people who live in this land; you must tear down their altars.’ Yet you have not obeyed me. What is this that you have done? So now I declare: I will not drive them out before you. They will become thorns in your sides, and their gods a trap for you.” As soon as the angel of the LORD finished speaking these words to all the Israelites, the people cried aloud and wept. They named that place Bochim, and they offered sacrifices there to the LORD.

Joshua’s generation and the next

Joshua had sent the people away, and the Israelites had gone, each to their own inheritance, to take possession of the land. The people served the LORD all through Joshua’s lifetime, and through the lifetime of the elders who lived on after him and had seen every great deed the LORD had done for Israel. Joshua son of Nun, the servant of the LORD, died at 110 years of age. They buried him within the borders of his own inheritance, at Timnath-heres, north of Mount Gaash in the hill country of Ephraim. That whole generation also died and was gathered to their ancestors, and after them another generation grew up who did not know the LORD or what he had done for Israel.

Israel serves the Baals

Then the Israelites did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and served the Baals. They abandoned the LORD, the God of their ancestors, who had brought them out of the land of Egypt. They followed other gods, gods of the peoples who lived around them, and bowed down to them, and so they made the LORD angry. They abandoned the LORD and served Baal and the Ashtaroth. Then the anger of the LORD blazed against Israel, and he gave them into the power of raiders, who plundered them. He sold them into the power of the enemies who surrounded them, and they could no longer hold their ground against their enemies. Every time they went out to fight, the hand of the LORD was against them to bring them disaster, just as the LORD had warned and had sworn to them. They were in great distress. Then the LORD raised up judges, who rescued them from the power of those who plundered them. Yet they would not listen even to their judges. They gave themselves like prostitutes to other gods and bowed down to them. They were quick to turn from the path their ancestors had walked, the path of obeying the commandments of the LORD; they did not do as their ancestors had done. Whenever the LORD raised up a judge for them, the LORD was with that judge and saved them from the power of their enemies as long as the judge lived. For the LORD was moved to pity when they groaned under those who oppressed and tormented them. But when the judge died, they would turn back and behave worse than their ancestors, following other gods, serving them and bowing down to them. They gave up none of their practices or their stubborn ways. Then the anger of the LORD blazed against Israel, and he said, “Since this nation has broken my covenant, which I commanded their ancestors to keep, and has not obeyed me, I in turn will no longer drive out before them any of the nations that Joshua left when he died, so that through them I may test Israel, to see whether they will keep to the way of the LORD and walk in it as their ancestors did, or not.” So the LORD let these nations remain. The LORD did not drive them out quickly, nor had he handed them over to Joshua.

fields.title: Judges 3
fields.body_html:
Nations left to test Israel

These are the nations that the LORD left in the land to test Israel by them, that is, all those in Israel who had never known any of the wars for Canaan. He did this only so that the generations of the Israelites would learn about war, at least those who had never experienced it before. These were the five rulers of the Philistines, all the Canaanites and Sidonians, and the Hivites living in the Lebanon mountains from Mount Baal-hermon to Lebo-hamath. They were left to test Israel, to find out whether the Israelites would obey the commandments of the LORD, which he had given their ancestors through Moses. The Israelites lived among the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites. They took the daughters of these peoples as wives, gave their own daughters to the sons of these peoples, and served their gods.

Othniel rescues Israel

The Israelites did what was evil in the sight of the LORD. They forgot the LORD their God, and they served the Baals and the Asherahs. So the anger of the LORD blazed against Israel, and he sold them into the power of Cushan-rishathaim king of Aram-naharaim. The Israelites served Cushan-rishathaim for eight years. Then the Israelites cried out to the LORD, and the LORD raised up a deliverer for them, who rescued them: Othniel son of Kenaz, Caleb’s younger brother. The Spirit of the LORD came on him, and he judged Israel. He went out to war, and the LORD gave Cushan-rishathaim king of Aram into his power, so that he overpowered Cushan-rishathaim. Then the land had peace for forty years, and Othniel son of Kenaz died.

Ehud and Eglon king of Moab

Once again the Israelites did what was evil in the sight of the LORD. So the LORD made Eglon king of Moab strong against Israel, because they had done what was evil in the sight of the LORD. Eglon gathered the Ammonites and the Amalekites to join him, and he went and defeated Israel, and they took over the City of Palms. The Israelites served Eglon king of Moab for eighteen years.

Then the Israelites cried out to the LORD, and the LORD raised up a deliverer for them: Ehud son of Gera, from the tribe of Benjamin, a left-handed man. The Israelites sent him to take their tribute to Eglon king of Moab. Ehud had made himself a double-edged sword, about 18 inches long, and he strapped it to his right thigh under his clothes. He presented the tribute to Eglon king of Moab. Eglon was an extremely fat man. When he had finished presenting the tribute, he sent away the people who had carried it. But Ehud himself turned back at the carved images near Gilgal and said, “Your Majesty, I have a secret message for you.” The king said, “Quiet!” and all his attendants went out. Ehud came to him as he sat alone in his cool upper room. Ehud said, “I have a message from God for you,” and the king rose from his seat. Ehud reached with his left hand, drew the sword from his right thigh, and drove it into the king’s belly. Even the handle went in after the blade, and the fat closed over the blade, because Ehud did not pull the sword out of his belly. And the point came out at his back. Then Ehud went out into the porch. He shut the doors of the upper room behind him and locked them. After Ehud had left, the king’s servants came in and found the upper room’s doors locked. They said, “He must be relieving himself in the cool room.” They waited until they were embarrassed, but he still did not open the doors of the upper room. So they took the key and opened them, and there was their master, lying dead on the floor. Ehud got away while they were waiting. He passed the carved images and escaped to Seirah. When he arrived, he blew the ram’s horn in the hill country of Ephraim, and the Israelites went down with him from the hills, with Ehud at their head. He told them, “Follow me, because the LORD has handed your enemies the Moabites over to you.” So they went down after him and took control of the fords of the Jordan leading to Moab, and they let no one cross. At that time they struck down about 10,000 Moabites, all of them sturdy and able fighters; not one got away. So Moab was brought under Israel’s power on that day, and the land had peace for eighty years.

Shamgar strikes the Philistines

After Ehud came Shamgar son of Anath. He struck down 600 Philistines with an ox goad, and he too rescued Israel.

fields.title: Judges 4
fields.body_html:
Jabin and Sisera oppress Israel

After Ehud had died, the Israelites again did what was evil in the sight of the LORD. So the LORD sold them into the power of Jabin, king of Canaan, who ruled in Hazor. The commander of his army was Sisera, who lived in Harosheth-hagoyim. The Israelites cried out to the LORD, because Jabin had 900 iron chariots and had oppressed the Israelites harshly for twenty years.

Deborah calls Barak to battle

Now Deborah, a prophet, the wife of Lappidoth, was judging Israel at that time. She used to hold court under the Palm of Deborah, in the hill country of Ephraim between Ramah and Bethel, and the Israelites came up to her to have their disputes decided. She sent and called for Barak son of Abinoam from Kedesh in Naphtali. She told him, “The LORD, the God of Israel, has given you this command: ‘Go, lead the way to Mount Tabor, and take 10,000 men from the tribes of Naphtali and Zebulun with you. I will draw Sisera, the commander of Jabin’s army, out to meet you at the Kishon River, with his chariots and his troops, and I will give him into your hand.’” Barak answered her, “If you go with me, I will go. But if you do not go with me, I will not go.” “I will certainly go with you,” she said. “But on the road you are taking, the honor will not be yours, for the LORD will hand Sisera over to a woman.” So Deborah set out with Barak for Kedesh. Barak called out the men of Zebulun and Naphtali to Kedesh, and 10,000 men marched up behind him. Deborah went up with him too. Now Heber the Kenite had separated from the Kenites, the descendants of Hobab, Moses’ father-in-law, and had pitched his tent as far away as the great tree in Zaanannim, near Kedesh. Word reached Sisera that Barak son of Abinoam had gone up Mount Tabor.

Sisera’s army at the Kishon

So Sisera called out all his chariots, 900 iron chariots, and all the troops who were with him, from Harosheth-hagoyim to the Kishon River. Then Deborah said to Barak, “Up! This is the day when the LORD has given Sisera into your hand. Is it not the LORD who has gone out ahead of you?” So Barak went down from Mount Tabor with 10,000 men following him. The LORD threw Sisera and all his chariots and all his army into panic before Barak’s attack with the sword. Sisera got down from his chariot and ran away on foot. Barak chased the chariots and the army all the way to Harosheth-hagoyim, and Sisera’s whole army fell by the sword. Not one man was left. Sisera, meanwhile, fled on foot to the tent of Jael, wife of Heber the Kenite, since Jabin king of Hazor and the family of Heber the Kenite were at peace. Jael came out to meet Sisera and said to him, “Come in, my lord, come in here with me. Do not be afraid.” So he went into the tent with her, and she covered him with a rug. He said to her, “Please let me have a little water to drink. I am thirsty.” So she opened a skin of milk, gave him a drink, and covered him again. He said to her, “Stand at the entrance of the tent. If anyone comes and asks you, ‘Is there a man here?’ tell him, ‘No.’” But Jael, Heber’s wife, took a tent peg, picked up a hammer, and crept up to him quietly. She drove the peg through his temple and into the ground. He was fast asleep from exhaustion, and he died. Just then Barak came by in pursuit of Sisera, and Jael went out to meet him. “Come,” she said to him, “I will show you the man you are looking for.” So he went in with her, and there was Sisera lying dead, the tent peg in his temple. So on that day God humbled Jabin king of Canaan before the Israelites. And the power of the Israelites pressed harder and harder against Jabin king of Canaan, until they had destroyed him.

fields.title: Judges 5
fields.body_html:
Deborah and Barak sing

That day Deborah and Barak son of Abinoam sang, and these were the words: “When long hair hung loose in Israel, when the people volunteered freely, bless the LORD! Listen, you kings; pay attention, you rulers! I will sing, I myself, to the LORD; I will make music to the LORD, the God of Israel. LORD, when you set out from Seir, when you strode out from the land of Edom, the earth shook, the skies poured, the clouds poured down water. The mountains quaked at the presence of the LORD, the One of Sinai, at the presence of the LORD, the God of Israel. In the time of Shamgar son of Anath, in the time of Jael, the highways lay empty, and travelers went by crooked side roads. The villages of Israel were deserted, deserted, until I, Deborah, arose, until I arose, a mother in Israel. Israel chose new gods; then war came to the city gates. Not a shield or spear was to be seen among forty thousand in Israel. My heart is with the commanders of Israel, who volunteered freely among the people. Bless the LORD! You who ride on white donkeys, you who sit on rich saddle cloths, and you who walk along the road, speak out! Over the voices of herders at the watering places, there they retell the righteous acts of the LORD, the righteous acts of his villagers in Israel. At that time the people of the LORD went down to their gates. Wake up, wake up, Deborah! Wake up, wake up, break into song! Rise up, Barak, son of Abinoam, and lead your captives away! Then the survivors came down, the people, to join the nobles; the LORD came down for me against the mighty. From Ephraim came those whose roots are in Amalek; after you, Benjamin, they came among your people. From Machir came down commanders, and from Zebulun those who carry the officer’s staff. The commanders of Issachar were with Deborah, and Issachar stood with Barak too, rushing into the valley at his heels. Among the divisions of Reuben there were great resolutions of heart. Why did you stay among the sheepfolds, listening to the shepherds whistling to their flocks? Among the divisions of Reuben there was great searching of heart. Gilead stayed across the Jordan. And Dan, why did he linger by the ships? Asher sat still along the seacoast, settled by his harbors. Zebulun was a people who held their lives cheap, ready to die, and so was Naphtali, on the high ground of the open field. The kings came and fought; the kings of Canaan fought then, at Taanach, by the streams of Megiddo, but they carried off no silver as plunder. From the heavens the fight was joined; the stars, along their courses, made war on Sisera. The Kishon River swept them off, the age-old river, the Kishon River. My soul, march on in strength! Then the horses’ hoofs hammered the ground as his strong steeds galloped and galloped. ‘Curse Meroz,’ says the angel of the LORD; ‘curse its people bitterly, because they did not come to help the LORD, to stand with him against the warriors.’ May Jael be blessed above all women, the wife of Heber the Kenite, blessed above all women who live in tents. He asked for water, and she gave milk; she served him curds in a bowl fit for princes. She reached out her hand for the tent peg, her right hand for the workman’s mallet. She struck Sisera and crushed his head; she broke through and pierced his temple. At her feet he sank down, he fell, he lay still; at her feet he sank down, he fell; at the place where he sank down, there he fell, slain. Through the window she looked out, Sisera’s mother, and cried through the lattice, ‘Why is his chariot taking so long to come? Why are the hoofbeats of his chariots so late?’ The wisest of her noble ladies answer her; she even gives herself the same answer: ‘They must be finding the spoil and sharing it out: a girl or two for every man; colored cloth as spoil for Sisera, colored cloth as spoil, richly embroidered, dyed cloth embroidered on both sides, for necks among the spoil.’ So may all your enemies perish, LORD! But may those who love him be like the sun as it rises in its strength.” And the land had peace for forty years.

fields.title: Judges 6
fields.body_html:
Midian oppresses Israel

The Israelites did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, and the LORD gave them into the power of Midian for seven years. Midian’s power weighed heavily on Israel. Because of Midian, the Israelites made themselves the hiding places in the mountains, and the caves and the strongholds. Whenever Israel had sown its crops, the Midianites and the Amalekites and the peoples of the east would come up and attack them. They would camp on their land and ruin the crops all the way to Gaza. They left nothing in Israel to live on, not a sheep, an ox or a donkey. They came up with their livestock and their tents, as thick as a swarm of locusts. There was no counting them or their camels, and they came into the land to lay it waste. Israel was reduced to great poverty because of Midian, and the Israelites cried out to the LORD.

When the Israelites cried out to the LORD because of Midian, the LORD sent a prophet to the Israelites, and he said to them, “This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘It was I who brought you up from Egypt and led you out of the house of slavery. I rescued you from the power of Egypt and from the power of everyone who oppressed you. I drove them out ahead of you and gave you their land. I said to you, “I am the LORD your God. You are not to fear the gods of the Amorites, though you live in their land.” But you have not listened to me.’”

The angel of the LORD calls Gideon

Then the angel of the LORD came to Ophrah and sat down under the terebinth there, which belonged to Joash the Abiezrite. Gideon, Joash’s son, was beating out wheat in the winepress so that the Midianites would not see it. The angel of the LORD appeared to him and said, “The LORD is with you, mighty warrior.” Gideon answered him, “Pardon me, my lord, but if the LORD is with us, why has all this come upon us? Where are all his wonders that our ancestors told us about when they said, ‘Did not the LORD bring us up from Egypt?’ Now the LORD has abandoned us and handed us over to Midian.” The LORD turned to him and said, “Go in this strength of yours, and you will save Israel from Midian’s power. Am I not the one sending you?” Gideon said to him, “Pardon me, my Lord, but how can I save Israel? My clan is the weakest in Manasseh, and I am the least in my family.” The LORD answered him, “I will be with you, and you will strike down the Midianites as if they were one man.” Gideon said to him, “If I have found favor with you, give me a sign that it is really you who are speaking to me. Please do not leave here until I come back to you and bring out my offering and set it before you.” He said, “I will stay until you come back.” Gideon went in and prepared a young goat, and unleavened bread from about 20 quarts of flour. He put the meat in a basket and the broth in a pot, brought them out to him under the terebinth, and set them before him.

The angel of God told him, “Take the meat and the unleavened bread, and place them on this rock. Then pour the broth out.” And he did so. Then the angel of the LORD reached out the tip of the staff in his hand and touched the meat and the unleavened bread. Fire flared up from the rock and burned up the meat and the bread, and the angel of the LORD vanished from his sight. When Gideon saw that it was the angel of the LORD, he cried out, “How terrible, Lord GOD! I have looked on the angel of the LORD face to face!” But the LORD said to him, “Peace to you! Do not be afraid; you will not die.” So Gideon built an altar to the LORD there and named it “The LORD Is Peace.” To this day it still stands in Ophrah of the Abiezrites.

Gideon tears down Baal’s altar

That same night the LORD said to him, “Take the young bull from your father’s herd, the second bull, the one seven years old. Tear down the altar of Baal that belongs to your father, and cut down the Asherah pole next to it. Then build an altar to the LORD your God on top of this stronghold, laid out in the proper way. Take the second bull and offer it as a burnt offering, using the wood of the Asherah pole that you cut down.” So Gideon took ten men from among his servants and did what the LORD had told him. But he was too afraid of his father’s family and the men of the town to do it by day, so he did it at night. When the men of the town got up early in the morning, they saw that Baal’s altar had been torn down and the Asherah pole beside it cut down, and that the second bull had been offered on the altar that had been built. They asked one another, “Who has done this?” After they had asked around and looked into it, they said, “Gideon son of Joash did it.” The men of the town said to Joash, “Bring your son out. He must die, for he has torn down the altar of Baal and cut down the Asherah pole that stood beside it.” But Joash said to all who stood against him, “Are you going to plead Baal’s case? Are you going to rescue him? By morning, anyone who pleads his case will be put to death! If Baal is a god, he should plead his own case, since it is his altar that has been torn down.” So on that day Gideon was given the name Jerubbaal, for it was said, “Let Baal contend against him, because he tore down his altar.”

Gideon calls out the tribes

Now all the Midianites and the Amalekites and the peoples of the east joined forces, crossed the Jordan, and camped in the Valley of Jezreel. Then the Spirit of the LORD clothed Gideon. He blew the ram’s horn, and the Abiezrites were called out to follow him. He sent messengers all through Manasseh, and they too were called out to follow him. He also sent messengers to Asher, Zebulun and Naphtali, and they came up to join them. Then Gideon said to God, “If you really mean to save Israel through me, as you have said, look, I am going to lay a wool fleece on the threshing floor. If dew falls on the fleece alone while all the ground stays dry, then I will be sure that you will save Israel through me, as you said.” And that is what happened. When he got up early the next morning, he squeezed the fleece and wrung enough dew out of it to fill a bowl with water. Then Gideon said to God, “Do not be angry with me, but let me speak just once more. Please let me make one more test with the fleece. This time let the fleece alone be dry, and let there be dew on all the ground.” That night God did so. Only the fleece was dry, and all the ground was covered with dew.

fields.title: Judges 7
fields.body_html:
Too many troops

Early in the morning Jerubbaal, that is, Gideon, and all the troops with him set up camp beside the spring of Harod. The camp of Midian lay to the north of them, by the hill of Moreh in the valley. The LORD said to Gideon, “You have too many troops with you for me to hand Midian over to them. Israel would only boast against me and say, ‘Our own strength has saved us.’ Now announce to the troops, ‘Whoever is afraid and trembling may turn back and leave Mount Gilead.’” So 22,000 of the troops turned back, and 10,000 were left.

But the LORD said to Gideon, “There are still too many troops. Take them down to the water. I will sift them there for you. When I tell you, ‘This one is to go with you,’ he will go with you. But when I tell you, ‘This one is not to go with you,’ he will not go.” So Gideon took the troops down to the water, and the LORD said to him, “Put everyone who laps up the water with his tongue, the way a dog laps, in one group. Put everyone who kneels down to drink in another.” The number of those who lapped, bringing the water to their mouths with their hands, was 300 men. All the rest of the troops knelt down to drink.

Then the LORD said to Gideon, “With the 300 men who lapped I will save you all, and I will hand Midian over to you. Let all the others go home.” The men who stayed took provisions in their hands, along with their rams’ horns. Gideon sent all the other men of Israel back to their tents, but he kept the 300 men. The camp of Midian lay below him in the valley.

A dream in the camp of Midian

That same night the LORD said to Gideon, “Get up and go down to attack the camp, because I have handed it over to you. But if you are afraid to attack, go down to the camp with Purah your servant, and listen to what they are saying. After that you will have the courage to attack the camp.” So he went down with Purah his servant to the outer edge of the armed men in the camp. The Midianites, the Amalekites and all the peoples of the east were spread across the valley as thick as locusts. Their camels were past counting, as many as the grains of sand by the sea. Just as Gideon arrived, one man was describing a dream to his friend. “Listen,” he said, “I had a dream. A round loaf of barley bread came rolling into the camp of Midian. It came to the tent and hit it so hard that it fell. It turned the tent upside down, and the tent collapsed.” His friend replied, “This can be nothing but the sword of Gideon son of Joash, the Israelite! God has handed Midian and the whole army over to him.”

When Gideon heard the dream and what it meant, he bowed down in worship. Then he went back to the camp of Israel and called out, “Get up! The LORD has handed the camp of Midian over to you.” He divided the 300 men into three companies and gave each of them a ram’s horn and an empty jar, with a torch inside the jar. “Watch me,” he told them, “and do what I do. When I reach the edge of the camp, do exactly as I do. When I blow my horn, along with everyone who is with me, you are to blow your horns too, on every side of the camp, and shout, ‘For the LORD and for Gideon!’”

Trumpets, jars and torches

Gideon and the 100 men with him reached the edge of the camp at the start of the middle watch of the night, just after the new guards had been posted. They blew their horns and smashed the jars they were holding. All three companies blew their horns and broke their jars. With the torches in their left hands and the horns for blowing in their right, they shouted, “A sword for the LORD and for Gideon!” Each man stood in his place around the camp, while the whole Midianite army ran about, shouting, and fled. When the 300 blew their horns, the LORD turned every man’s sword against his comrade throughout the whole army. The army fled toward Zererah as far as Beth-shittah, and as far as the edge of Abel-meholah near Tabbath. Then the men of Israel from Naphtali, Asher and all Manasseh were called to arms, and they chased the Midianites. Gideon sent messengers all through the hill country of Ephraim with this message: “Come down against the Midianites and take the waters ahead of them as far as Beth-barah, and the Jordan as well.” So all the men of Ephraim were called out, and they took the waters as far as Beth-barah, and the Jordan. They also captured the two commanders of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb. Oreb they killed at the Rock of Oreb, and Zeeb at the Winepress of Zeeb. They kept up the pursuit of the Midianites, and they brought the heads of Oreb and Zeeb to Gideon from across the Jordan.

fields.title: Judges 8
fields.body_html:
Gideon answers Ephraim

Then the men of Ephraim said to Gideon, “Why have you treated us like this? You did not call us when you went out to fight Midian!” And they argued with him sharply. He answered them, “What have I done, compared with you? Are not the grapes Ephraim gleans better than the whole harvest of Abiezer? God handed the commanders of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb, over to you. What was I able to do compared with you?” When he said this, their anger against him cooled. Gideon came to the Jordan and crossed it, he and the 300 men with him, exhausted but still pursuing. He said to the men of Succoth, “Please give some loaves of bread to the troops who follow me, for they are exhausted, and I am pursuing Zebah and Zalmunna, the kings of Midian.” But the officials of Succoth said, “Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna already in your grip, that we should give bread to your army?” Gideon said, “Very well. When the LORD hands Zebah and Zalmunna over to me, I will thresh your flesh with thorns of the wilderness and with briers.” From there he went up to Penuel and made the same request, and the men of Penuel gave him the same answer as the men of Succoth. So he said to the men of Penuel as well, “When I come back safe and sound, I will tear down this tower.”

Zebah and Zalmunna captured

Zebah and Zalmunna were at Karkor with their forces, about 15,000 men. These were all that were left of the whole army of the eastern peoples; 120,000 swordsmen had fallen. Gideon went up by the route of the tent dwellers, east of Nobah and Jogbehah, and attacked the camp while it felt secure. Zebah and Zalmunna fled, but he chased after them and captured the two kings of Midian, Zebah and Zalmunna, and threw their whole army into panic. Then Gideon son of Joash came back from the battle by the Heres pass. He caught a young man from Succoth and questioned him, and the young man wrote down for him the officials and elders of Succoth, seventy-seven men. Then he came to the men of Succoth and said, “Look: Zebah and Zalmunna! You taunted me about them when you said, ‘Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna already in your grip, that we should give bread to your exhausted men?’” He took the elders of the town, and with thorns of the wilderness and briers he taught the men of Succoth a lesson. He also tore down the tower of Penuel and killed the men of the town. Then he said to Zebah and Zalmunna, “What about the men you killed at Tabor?” They replied, “They were like you, every one of them with the look of a king’s son.” He said, “They were my brothers, my own mother’s sons. As surely as the LORD lives, had you spared their lives, I would not kill you.” Then he said to Jether, his firstborn son, “Get up and kill them!” But the boy did not draw his sword. He was afraid, because he was still young. Zebah and Zalmunna said, “Get up and strike us down yourself, for as the man is, so is his strength.” Gideon rose and killed Zebah and Zalmunna, then took the crescent ornaments from their camels’ necks. Then the men of Israel said to Gideon, “Rule over us, you and your son and your grandson too, for you have saved us from the power of Midian.” But Gideon said to them, “I will not rule over you, and my son will not rule over you. The LORD will rule over you.” Then Gideon said to them, “I do have one request: let each of you give me a ring from his plunder.” The enemy had worn gold rings, because they were Ishmaelites. “We will gladly give them,” they answered. So they spread out a cloak, and each man threw onto it a ring from his plunder. The gold rings he had asked for weighed about 42 1/2 pounds. That was besides the crescent ornaments, the pendants and the purple clothing worn by the kings of Midian, and besides the chains on their camels’ necks. Gideon made the gold into an ephod and set it up in his town, Ophrah. There all Israel prostituted themselves by worshiping it, and it became a trap for Gideon and his family. So Midian was humbled before the Israelites and did not raise its head again, and the land had peace for forty years in the days of Gideon.

Gideon’s last years

Jerubbaal son of Joash went back and lived in his own house. Gideon had seventy sons who were his own offspring, for he had many wives. His concubine who lived in Shechem bore him a son as well, and he named him Abimelech. Gideon son of Joash died at a good old age and was buried in his father Joash’s tomb at Ophrah of the Abiezrites.

As soon as Gideon was dead, the Israelites turned away again and prostituted themselves to the Baals. They made Baal-berith their god. The Israelites did not remember the LORD their God, who had rescued them from the power of all the enemies around them. Nor did they show faithful love to the family of Jerubbaal, that is, Gideon, in return for all the good he had done for Israel.

fields.title: Judges 9
fields.body_html:
Abimelech kills his brothers

Abimelech son of Jerubbaal went to his mother’s relatives in Shechem and spoke to them and to the whole clan of his mother’s family. He said, “Please put this question to all the leaders of Shechem: ‘Which is better for you, to be ruled by seventy men, all the sons of Jerubbaal, or to be ruled by one man? Remember that I am your own flesh and blood.’” His mother’s relatives spoke on his behalf and put all these words before the leaders of Shechem, and their hearts leaned toward Abimelech, because they said, “He is our own kin.” They gave him seventy pieces of silver from the temple of Baal-berith, and with that money Abimelech hired worthless, reckless men, who became his followers. He went to his father’s home at Ophrah and killed his brothers, the seventy sons of Jerubbaal, on a single stone. But Jotham, Jerubbaal’s youngest son, survived because he had gone into hiding.

Jotham speaks from Mount Gerizim

Then all the leaders of Shechem and all of Beth-millo came together and went and made Abimelech king beside the oak of the standing stone at Shechem. When Jotham was told about it, he went and stood on the summit of Mount Gerizim and shouted out to them, “Listen to me, leaders of Shechem, so that God will listen to you. One day the trees set out to anoint a king to rule them. They went to the olive tree and said, ‘Be our king.’ But the olive tree answered them, ‘Should I stop giving my rich oil, which is used to honor God and humans, and go to wave over the trees?’ Then the trees said to the fig tree, ‘You come and be our king.’ But the fig tree answered them, ‘Should I give up my sweetness and my fine fruit and go to wave over the trees?’ Then the trees said to the vine, ‘You come and be our king.’ But the vine answered them, ‘Should I give up my new wine, which brings joy to God and humans, and go to wave over the trees?’ Then all the trees said to the bramble, ‘You come and be our king.’ The bramble answered the trees, ‘If you are truly anointing me king over you, come and shelter in my shade. Otherwise, may fire come out of the bramble and burn up the cedars of Lebanon!’ So now, if you acted faithfully and honorably when you made Abimelech king, and if you have treated Jerubbaal and his family well and given him what his deeds deserved— for my father fought for you, risked his life, and rescued you from the power of Midian, but today you have turned against my father’s family. You have killed his sons, seventy men, on a single stone, and made Abimelech, the son of his slave woman, king over the leaders of Shechem because he is your relative— if, I say, you have acted faithfully and honorably toward Jerubbaal and his family today, then be happy with Abimelech, and may he be happy with you. But if not, may fire come out from Abimelech and burn up the leaders of Shechem and Beth-millo, and may fire come out from the leaders of Shechem and Beth-millo and burn up Abimelech!” Then Jotham ran for his life. He escaped to Beer and settled there, out of the reach of his brother Abimelech.

Shechem turns against Abimelech

Abimelech held power over Israel for three years. Then God sent an evil spirit to come between Abimelech and the leaders of Shechem, and the leaders of Shechem broke faith with Abimelech, so that the violence done to the seventy sons of Jerubbaal would come back on those who did it, and the guilt for their blood would fall on their brother Abimelech, who killed them, and on the leaders of Shechem, who helped him kill his brothers. The leaders of Shechem set men in ambush against him on the mountaintops, and they robbed everyone who came past them along the road. Abimelech was told about it.

Then Gaal son of Ebed arrived with his relatives and moved into Shechem, and the leaders of Shechem came to trust him. They went out to the fields, harvested the grapes from their vineyards and trod them, and held a harvest festival. They went into the temple of their god, ate and drank, and cursed Abimelech. Gaal son of Ebed said, “Who is Abimelech, and what is Shechem, that we should be his servants? Is he not Jerubbaal’s son, with Zebul as his deputy? Serve the men of Hamor, Shechem’s father! Why should we serve Abimelech? If only this people were under my command! I would get rid of Abimelech.” And he said to Abimelech, “Build up your army and come out and fight!” When Zebul, the governor of the city, heard what Gaal son of Ebed had said, he was furious. He secretly sent messengers to Abimelech to say, “Gaal son of Ebed and his relatives have come to Shechem, and they are turning the city against you. So now, set out during the night, you and the troops with you, and lie in ambush in the open country. In the morning, as soon as the sun is up, get up early and charge the city. When he and his men come out against you, deal with him however the moment allows.”

So Abimelech and all the troops with him set out by night and took up hidden positions around Shechem in four companies. Gaal son of Ebed went out and was standing at the entrance to the city gate when Abimelech and his troops rose up from their hiding places. When Gaal saw the troops, he said to Zebul, “Look, there are people coming down from the mountaintops!” Zebul answered, “You are taking the shadows of the mountains for men.”

Gaal spoke again: “Look, troops are coming down from the center of the land, and another company is coming by the road from the Soothsayers’ Oak!” Then Zebul said to him, “Where is your big talk now, you who said, ‘Who is Abimelech, that we should be his servants?’ Are these not the men you looked down on? Go out now and fight them!”

So Gaal went out at the head of the leaders of Shechem and fought Abimelech. Abimelech chased him, and Gaal ran from him. Many fell dead along the way, right up to the entrance of the gate. Abimelech then stayed at Arumah, and Zebul drove Gaal and his relatives out, so that they could no longer live in Shechem. On the following day the people of Shechem came out to the fields, and someone reported it to Abimelech. He took his troops, split them into three companies, and set an ambush in the fields. As soon as he saw people leaving the city, he rose and attacked them. Abimelech and the forces with him charged forward and took their stand at the entrance to the city gate, while the other two companies charged at everyone in the fields and struck them down. Abimelech fought against the city all that day. He captured it and killed the people in it; then he tore the city down and scattered salt over it.

When all the leaders of the Tower of Shechem heard this, they went into the stronghold of the temple of El-berith. Abimelech was told that all the leaders of the Tower of Shechem had gathered there. Abimelech and all his troops went up Mount Zalmon. He took an axe in his hand, cut a branch from the trees, lifted it up and put it on his shoulder. Then he said to the men with him, “Quick! Do just what you have seen me do!” So all the troops also cut down a branch each and followed Abimelech. They piled the branches against the stronghold and set it on fire over the people inside. So all the people of the Tower of Shechem died too, about 1,000 men and women.

Abimelech dies at Thebez

Next Abimelech went to Thebez, laid siege to it, and captured it. But inside the city stood a strong tower, and all the men and women and all the leaders of the city fled into it. They shut themselves in and climbed up onto the roof of the tower. Abimelech came up to the tower and attacked it. He went right up to the entrance of the tower to set it on fire. But a woman dropped an upper millstone on Abimelech’s head and cracked his skull. He quickly called to the young man who carried his armor and said to him, “Draw your sword and kill me, so that no one can say of me, ‘A woman killed him.’” So his young man ran him through, and he died. When the men of Israel saw that Abimelech was dead, they all went back home. In this way God paid Abimelech back for the evil he had done to his father by murdering his seventy brothers. God also brought all the evil of the men of Shechem back on their own heads, and the curse of Jotham son of Jerubbaal came upon them.

fields.title: Judges 10
fields.body_html:
Tola and Jair

After Abimelech, Tola son of Puah, son of Dodo, rose up to save Israel. He was a man of Issachar, and he lived at Shamir in the hill country of Ephraim. He judged Israel for twenty-three years. Then he died and was buried in Shamir.

After him came Jair the Gileadite, who judged Israel for twenty-two years. Jair had thirty sons, riding thirty donkeys, and they owned thirty towns. Those towns in the land of Gilead are known as Havvoth-jair to this day. Then Jair died and was buried in Kamon.

Israel cries out under the Ammonites

Once again the Israelites did what was evil in the sight of the LORD. They served the Baals and the Ashtaroth, the gods of Aram, the gods of Sidon, the gods of Moab, the gods of the Ammonites and the gods of the Philistines. They abandoned the LORD and no longer served him. Then the anger of the LORD blazed against Israel, and he sold them into the power of the Philistines and into the power of the Ammonites. That year they shattered and crushed the Israelites, and for eighteen years they oppressed all the Israelites who lived east of the Jordan in Gilead, the land of the Amorites. The Ammonites even crossed the Jordan to make war on Judah, on Benjamin and on the house of Ephraim. Israel was in great distress. Then the Israelites cried out to the LORD: “We have sinned against you, because we have abandoned our God and served the Baals.”

And the LORD said to the Israelites, “Did I not save you from the Egyptians, the Amorites, the Ammonites and the Philistines? When the Sidonians, the Amalekites and the Maonites oppressed you and you cried out to me, I saved you from their power. Yet you have abandoned me and served other gods. So I will not save you again. Go and cry to the gods you chose for yourselves. Let them be the ones to save you when trouble comes.” But the Israelites said to the LORD, “We have sinned. Deal with us in whatever way you think best, but please rescue us today.” Then they got rid of the foreign gods that were among them and served the LORD, and he could bear Israel’s misery no longer.

Gilead looks for a leader

When the Ammonites were called to arms, they made camp in Gilead, while the Israelites came together and made camp at Mizpah. The people and the officials of Gilead asked one another, “Who will be the man to open the fight against the Ammonites? He will be head over everyone who lives in Gilead.”

fields.title: Judges 11
fields.body_html:
Jephthah the Gileadite

Jephthah the Gileadite was a strong warrior. He was the son of a prostitute, and his father was Gilead. Gilead’s wife also bore him sons. When they grew up, they drove Jephthah away and told him, “You will have no share in our father’s estate, because you are the son of another woman.” So Jephthah escaped from his brothers and made his home in the land of Tob. A band of worthless men gathered around him and went out raiding with him.

Some time later the Ammonites went to war against Israel. When the Ammonites were fighting against Israel, the elders of Gilead went to bring Jephthah back from the land of Tob. They said to Jephthah, “Come and be our commander, so that we can fight the Ammonites.” But Jephthah said to the elders of Gilead, “Was it not you who hated me and drove me out of my father’s house? Why come to me now, when you are in trouble?” The elders of Gilead answered Jephthah, “That is exactly why we have come back to you now. Come with us and fight the Ammonites, and you will be our head, ruling over everyone who lives in Gilead.” Jephthah answered the elders of Gilead, “If you bring me back to make war on the Ammonites and the LORD hands them over to me, then I will be your head.” The elders of Gilead said to Jephthah, “the LORD is witness between us. We will certainly do as you say.” So Jephthah went back with the elders of Gilead, and the people set him over themselves as head and commander. And Jephthah repeated all his terms before the LORD at Mizpah.

Jephthah’s message to the king of Ammon

Then Jephthah sent messengers to the king of the Ammonites with this question: “What quarrel do you have with me, that you have come to attack my land?” The king of the Ammonites answered Jephthah’s messengers, “Because Israel took my land when they came up from Egypt, all the way from the Arnon to the Jabbok and to the Jordan. Now give it back peacefully.” Jephthah sent messengers once more to the king of the Ammonites, and they said to him, “This is what Jephthah says: Israel did not take the land of Moab or the land of the Ammonites. When Israel came up from Egypt, it journeyed through the wilderness as far as the Red Sea and then reached Kadesh. Israel sent messengers to ask the king of Edom, ‘Please allow us to cross your land.’ But the king of Edom paid no attention. They sent the same request to the king of Moab, and he refused too. So Israel remained at Kadesh. Then Israel traveled through the wilderness and went around the lands of Edom and Moab. They passed along the east side of Moab and camped on the far side of the Arnon. They did not enter Moabite territory, because the Arnon was the border of Moab. Then Israel sent messengers to Sihon king of the Amorites, who ruled at Heshbon, and said to him, ‘Please allow us to cross your land to our own place.’ But Sihon did not trust Israel to pass through his territory. He gathered all his forces, camped at Jahaz and attacked Israel. Then the LORD, the God of Israel, gave Sihon and all his forces into Israel’s power, and Israel defeated them and took possession of the whole land of the Amorites who lived in that region. They took over the whole Amorite territory, from the Arnon in the south to the Jabbok, and from the wilderness across to the Jordan. So now that the LORD, the God of Israel, has driven out the Amorites before his people Israel, are you to take their land? Do you not take possession of whatever your god Chemosh gives you? In the same way, we will possess all the land of those whom the LORD our God has driven out before us. Are you really a better man than Balak son of Zippor, king of Moab? Did he ever dispute with Israel or make war on them? Israel has lived in Heshbon and its villages, in Aroer and its villages, and in all the towns along the Arnon for 300 years. Why did you not take them back during all that time? I have not wronged you, but you are wronging me by making war on me. Let the LORD, who is the Judge, settle the case today between the Israelites and the Ammonites.” But the king of the Ammonites paid no attention to the message Jephthah sent him.

Jephthah makes a vow

Then the Spirit of the LORD came on Jephthah. He went through Gilead and Manasseh, passed through Mizpah of Gilead, and from Mizpah of Gilead he went on against the Ammonites. And Jephthah made a vow to the LORD: “If you will truly hand the Ammonites over to me, then whoever or whatever comes out through the doors of my house to meet me as I come home safe from the Ammonites will be the LORD’s, and I will sacrifice it as a burnt offering.”

So Jephthah crossed over to the Ammonites to fight them, and the LORD handed them over to him. He defeated them with a great slaughter from Aroer to the area of Minnith, twenty towns, and as far as Abel-keramim. So the Ammonites were brought under the power of the Israelites.

Jephthah’s daughter comes out to meet him

When Jephthah reached his home in Mizpah, out came his daughter to meet him, dancing to the beat of tambourines. She was his one and only child; apart from her he had no son or daughter. As soon as he saw her, he tore his clothes and cried, “Oh, my daughter! You have struck me down! You have become the one who brings ruin on me. I have given my word to the LORD, and I cannot go back on it.” She said to him, “My father, you have given your word to the LORD. Do to me what you have promised, now that the LORD has brought justice for you on your enemies the Ammonites.” She also said to her father, “Grant me this one request. Give me two months to go off into the hills with my friends and weep there, because I will never marry.” “Go,” he said, and he let her go for two months. She went with her friends into the hills and mourned that she would never marry. At the end of two months she came back to her father, and he did to her what he had vowed. She had never had relations with a man. And it became a custom in Israel. Every year the young women of Israel would go out for four days to commemorate the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite.

fields.title: Judges 12
fields.body_html:
Jephthah and the men of Ephraim

The men of Ephraim were called to arms, and they crossed over to Zaphon. They said to Jephthah, “Why did you cross over to fight the Ammonites and not call us to go along? We will burn your house over your head!” Jephthah answered them, “My people and I were in a bitter struggle with the Ammonites. I called you, but you did not rescue me from their power. When I saw that you would not save me, I took my life in my hands and crossed over to fight the Ammonites, and the LORD handed them over to me. So why have you come up against me today to fight with me?” Then Jephthah gathered all the men of Gilead and fought against Ephraim. The men of Gilead defeated Ephraim, because the Ephraimites had said, “You Gileadites are nothing but runaways from Ephraim, living among Ephraim and Manasseh.” The Gileadites took control of the fords of the Jordan to cut off Ephraim. Whenever one of the Ephraimites who were escaping said, “Let me cross,” the men of Gilead would ask him, “Are you an Ephraimite?” If he answered, “No,” they would say to him, “Then say ‘Shibboleth.’” He would say “Sibboleth,” because he could not pronounce the word correctly. Then they would seize him and kill him there at the Jordan fords. At that time 42,000 Ephraimites fell. Jephthah judged Israel for six years. Then Jephthah the Gileadite died and was buried in one of the towns of Gilead.

Ibzan, Elon and Abdon

After him, Ibzan of Bethlehem judged Israel. He had thirty sons and thirty daughters. He gave his daughters in marriage outside his clan, and brought in thirty young women from outside as wives for his sons. He judged Israel for seven years. Then Ibzan died and was buried in Bethlehem.

After him, Elon the Zebulunite judged Israel. He judged Israel for ten years. Then Elon the Zebulunite died and was buried in Aijalon in the land of Zebulun.

After him, Abdon son of Hillel the Pirathonite judged Israel. His forty sons and thirty grandsons rode on seventy donkeys. He judged Israel for eight years. Then Abdon son of Hillel the Pirathonite died and was buried at Pirathon in the land of Ephraim, in the hill country of the Amalekites.

fields.title: Judges 13
fields.body_html:
The Philistines rule over Israel

Once more the Israelites did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, and the LORD gave them into the power of the Philistines for forty years.

A son promised to Manoah’s wife

There was a man from Zorah, of the clan of the Danites, whose name was Manoah. His wife was unable to conceive and had borne no children. The angel of the LORD appeared to the woman. “Listen,” he told her, “you are unable to conceive and have borne no children, but you will conceive and bear a son. So now be careful: drink no wine or beer, and eat nothing unclean. For you will conceive and give birth to a son. No razor is to touch his head, because the boy will be a Nazirite, set apart to God from the womb. He will begin to save Israel from the power of the Philistines.” The woman went to her husband and said, “A man of God has come to me. He looked like the angel of God, very awe-inspiring. I did not ask where he was from, and he did not give me his name. But he said to me, ‘You will conceive and give birth to a son. So now, drink no wine or beer, and eat nothing unclean, for the boy is to be a Nazirite, set apart to God from the womb until the day he dies.’”

Manoah asks for the man of God to return

Then Manoah prayed to the LORD: “Please, my Lord, let the man of God whom you sent come to us again and teach us what we should do for the boy who is to be born.” God listened to Manoah, and the angel of God came to the woman again while she was sitting in the field. But Manoah her husband was not with her. The woman ran quickly to tell her husband. “Look,” she said to him, “the man who came to me the other day has appeared to me again.” Manoah got up and followed his wife. When he reached the man, he asked, “Are you the one who spoke to my wife?” “I am,” he answered. Then Manoah said, “Now when your words come true, what is to be the boy’s way of life, and what will his work be?” The angel of the LORD said to Manoah, “Your wife must be careful to do all that I told her. She must not eat anything that comes from the grapevine, or drink wine or beer, or eat anything unclean. She must keep everything I have commanded her.” Manoah said to the angel of the LORD, “Please stay with us, so that we can prepare a young goat for you to eat.” The angel of the LORD answered Manoah, “Even if you hold me back, I will eat none of your food. If you want to prepare a burnt offering, offer it to the LORD.” For Manoah had not realized that he was the angel of the LORD. Manoah then said to the angel of the LORD, “What is your name? We would like to honor you when your words come true.” The angel of the LORD answered him, “Why do you ask about my name? It is wonderful.” So Manoah took the young goat along with the grain offering and offered them to the LORD on the rock. Then, while Manoah and his wife watched, the angel did a wonderful thing. As the flame rose from the altar toward the sky, the angel of the LORD went up in the flame from the altar. When Manoah and his wife saw it, they fell face down on the ground. The angel of the LORD appeared no more to Manoah and his wife. Then Manoah realized that it had been the angel of the LORD. Manoah said to his wife, “We are certain to die, because we have seen God!” But his wife answered him, “If the LORD had meant to kill us, he would not have accepted a burnt offering and a grain offering from our hands.
