He would not have shown us all these things, or let us hear such things now.” In time the woman bore a son, and she named him Samson. As the boy grew up, the LORD blessed him. Then the Spirit of the LORD began to drive him on at Mahaneh-dan, between Zorah and Eshtaol.

fields.title: Judges 14
fields.body_html:
Samson and the woman of Timnah

Samson went down to Timnah, and in Timnah he noticed one of the young Philistine women. He came back up and told his father and mother, “I have seen a woman in Timnah, one of the young Philistine women. Now get her for me as my wife.” His father and mother said to him, “Is there not a woman among your relatives or anywhere among my people? Must you go and take a wife from the uncircumcised Philistines?” But Samson said to his father, “Get her for me. She is the one who looks right to me.” His father and mother did not know that this came from the LORD, for he was looking for an opportunity to act against the Philistines. At that time the Philistines were ruling over Israel.

The lion and the riddle

Then Samson went down to Timnah with his father and mother. When they reached the vineyards of Timnah, a young lion suddenly came at him, roaring. The Spirit of the LORD rushed on him, and with nothing in his hands he ripped the lion apart as easily as one rips apart a young goat. Yet he told neither his father nor his mother what he had done. Then he went down and talked with the woman, and she looked right to Samson. Some time later he went back to marry her, and he turned aside to look at the lion’s carcass. There in the lion’s body was a swarm of bees, and honey. He scooped the honey out into his hands and went on, eating as he walked. When he reached his father and mother, he gave them some, and they ate. Yet he did not tell them he had scooped the honey out of the lion’s carcass. His father went down to see the woman, and Samson held a feast there, as young men used to do. When the people there saw him, they brought thirty companions to be with him. Samson said to them, “Let me give you a riddle. If you can explain it to me during the seven days of the feast and work it out, I will give you thirty linen garments and thirty sets of festive clothes. But if you cannot tell me, then you must give me thirty linen garments and thirty sets of festive clothes.” They said to him, “Tell us your riddle. Let us hear it.” He said to them, “From the one who eats came food; from the strong one came something sweet.” For three days they could not explain the riddle. On the seventh day they said to Samson’s wife, “Coax your husband into telling us the riddle, or we will set fire to you and your father’s household. Did you invite us here to rob us? Is that it?” Samson’s wife wept over him and said, “You only hate me; you do not love me at all. You have given my people a riddle, and you have not told me the answer.” He said to her, “Look, I have not told even my father or my mother. Why should I tell you?” She wept over him all through the seven days of their feast. On the seventh day he told her, because she kept pressing him, and she explained the riddle to her people. On the seventh day, before the sun went down, the men of the city said to him, “What is sweeter than honey? What is stronger than a lion?” Samson answered them, “If you had not plowed with my heifer, you would never have worked out my riddle.” Then the Spirit of the LORD rushed on him. He went down to Ashkelon, struck down thirty of their men, stripped them of their clothes, and gave the sets of clothing to those who had explained the riddle. Burning with anger, he went back up to his father’s house.

Then Samson’s wife was given to his companion, the one who had served as his best man.

fields.title: Judges 15
fields.body_html:
Samson burns the Philistines’ grain

Some time later, at the time of the wheat harvest, Samson went to visit his wife, taking a young goat with him. He said, “I am going in to my wife in her room.” But her father would not let him go in. Her father said, “I was sure that you hated her completely, so I gave her to your companion. Is not her younger sister more beautiful than she is? Please take her instead.” Samson said to them, “This time no one can blame me when I do the Philistines harm.” So Samson went and caught 300 foxes. He took torches, tied the foxes together in pairs, tail to tail, and set a torch in the middle, between the two tails of every pair. He set the torches on fire and let the foxes loose in the Philistines’ standing grain. He burned up everything, from the stacked sheaves to the uncut grain, and the vineyards and olive groves as well. The Philistines asked, “Who did this?” They were told, “Samson, the Timnite’s son-in-law, because the man took his wife and gave her to his companion.” So the Philistines went up and burned her to death, and her father with her. Samson said to them, “Since you have acted like this, I swear I will take revenge on you, and only after that will I stop.” He struck them down hip and thigh, a great slaughter. Then he went down and stayed in the cleft of the rock of Etam.

The jawbone of a donkey

Then the Philistines went up, camped in Judah, and spread out around Lehi. The men of Judah asked, “Why have you come to attack us?” They answered, “We have come to take Samson prisoner, to do to him what he did to us.” Then 3,000 men of Judah went down to the cleft in the rock of Etam and said to Samson, “Do you not know that we are ruled by the Philistines? What is this you have brought on us?” He answered them, “I only did to them what they did to me.” They told him, “We have come down to tie you up and hand you over to the Philistines.” Then Samson said, “Give me your oath that you yourselves will not attack me.” “No,” they told him, “we will only tie you up and hand you over to them. We will certainly not kill you.” So they tied him with two new ropes and took him up out of the cleft in the rock. As he came to Lehi, the Philistines ran shouting to meet him. Then the Spirit of the LORD rushed on him. The ropes on his arms became like flax caught in a fire, and his bonds melted away from his hands. He came upon the fresh jawbone of a donkey. He reached out and took hold of it, and with it he struck down 1,000 men. Then Samson said, “With a donkey’s jawbone, a heap, two heaps of them; with a donkey’s jawbone I struck down a thousand men!” When he had finished speaking, he threw the jawbone away, and that place was called Ramath-lehi. He was very thirsty, and he called out to the LORD, “You have given this great victory by the hand of your servant. Now must I die of thirst and fall into the power of these uncircumcised men?” So God split open the hollow at Lehi, and water flowed from it. Samson drank, his strength came back, and he revived. That is why he named it En-hakkore. It is still there at Lehi to this day. In the days of the Philistines, Samson judged Israel for twenty years.

fields.title: Judges 16
fields.body_html:
Samson at Gaza

Samson went to Gaza. There he saw a prostitute, and he went in and slept with her. The people of Gaza were told, “Samson has come here!” So they surrounded the place and lay in ambush for him at the city gate through the night. They made no move the whole night, for they said, “When morning light comes, we will kill him.” But Samson lay there only until midnight. At midnight he got up and seized the doors of the city gate together with its two posts, and he tore them loose, bar and all. Lifting them onto his shoulders, he carried them all the way up to the hilltop that faces Hebron.

Delilah and the secret of Samson’s strength

Some time after this, he fell in love with a woman named Delilah, in the Valley of Sorek. The rulers of the Philistines came up to her and said, “Coax him, and find out what makes his strength so great and how we can overpower him, so that we can tie him up and subdue him. Each of us will give you about 28 pounds of silver.” So Delilah said to Samson, “Please tell me what makes your strength so great, and what it would take to tie you up and subdue you.” Samson answered, “Suppose they tie me with seven fresh bowstrings that were never dried. Then I will become weak and be like any other man.” So the Philistine rulers brought up to her seven fresh bowstrings, never dried, and she tied him up with them. She had men hidden in the inner room, waiting. Then she said to him, “Samson, the Philistines are upon you!” But he snapped the bowstrings as easily as a strand of flax fiber snaps at the touch of fire. So the secret of his strength was still not found out. Then Delilah said to Samson, “You have made a fool of me and told me lies! Now please tell me what it would take to tie you up.” He said to her, “If they tie me up tightly with new ropes that have never been used for work, I will become weak and be like any other man.” So Delilah took new ropes and tied him up with them. Then she said to him, “Samson, the Philistines are upon you!” Men were hidden in the inner room, waiting. But he snapped the ropes off his arms like thread. Then Delilah said to Samson, “All this time you have been making a fool of me and telling me lies. Tell me what it would take to tie you up.” He answered, “Weave the seven braids of my head into the fabric on the loom.” So she wove his hair in and fastened it tight with the pin, and said to him, “Samson, the Philistines are upon you!” He woke from his sleep and pulled out the pin of the loom along with the web. Then she said to him, “How can you tell me, ‘I love you,’ while you keep your heart from me? Three times now you have made a fool of me, and you still have not told me what makes your strength so great.” Day after day she kept pressing him with her words and pleading with him, until he was weary to death of it. So he told her everything that was in his heart. “No razor has ever touched my head,” he said to her, “because from my mother’s womb I have been set apart to God as a Nazirite. If my head were shaved, my strength would leave me, and I would become weak and be like any other man.” When Delilah saw that he had told her everything in his heart, she sent word to the rulers of the Philistines: “Come up just once more, for he has told me everything.” So the rulers of the Philistines came up to her, bringing the silver with them. She lulled him to sleep on her lap and called for a man, and she had the seven braids of his head shaved off. Then she began to subdue him, and his strength had left him. Then she said, “Samson, the Philistines are upon you!” He woke from his sleep and said, “I will go out as I did the other times and shake myself loose.” But he did not know that the LORD had left him. The Philistines seized him and gouged out his eyes. They took him down to Gaza and bound him with bronze shackles, and he was set to grinding grain in the prison. But the hair of his head began to grow again after it had been shaved.

Samson brings down the house of Dagon

Now the rulers of the Philistines assembled to offer a great sacrifice to their god Dagon and to celebrate. They said, “Our god has given into our hands Samson our enemy.” When the people saw him, they praised their god. They said, “Our god has given into our hands our enemy, the one who laid waste our land and killed so many of us.” When they were in high spirits, they said, “Call for Samson, and let him entertain us.” So they called Samson out of the prison, and he performed for them. They had him stand between the pillars. Samson said to the young man who was leading him by the hand, “Let me rest here and feel the pillars that hold up the temple, so that I can lean against them.” The temple was full of men and women, and all the rulers of the Philistines were there. On the roof there were about 3,000 men and women looking on as Samson performed. Then Samson called out to the LORD: “Lord GOD, please remember me. Please give me strength just this once more, O God, so that with one blow I may pay the Philistines back for my two eyes.” Samson took hold of the two middle pillars on which the temple stood, and he braced himself against them, his right hand on one and his left hand on the other. And Samson said, “Let me die together with the Philistines!” He pushed with all his might, and down came the temple on the rulers and on all the people inside. So he killed more people by his death than he had killed during his whole life. Then his brothers and all his father’s family came down. They took him and brought him back up, and they buried him in the tomb of Manoah his father, between Zorah and Eshtaol. He had judged Israel for twenty years.

fields.title: Judges 17
fields.body_html:
Micah’s carved image

There was a man from the hill country of Ephraim whose name was Micah. He said to his mother, “You know the about 28 pounds of silver that was taken from you, and how you pronounced a curse over it, and I heard you say it? Look, I have the silver. I am the one who took it.” His mother said, “May the LORD bless my son!” When he gave the about 28 pounds of silver back to his mother, she said, “I solemnly dedicate this silver to the LORD from my own hand, for my son, to make a carved image and a cast idol. So now I will give it back to you.” So he returned the silver to his mother, and she took about 5 pounds of silver and gave it to a silversmith. He made it into a carved image and a cast idol, and it was kept in Micah’s house. Now this man Micah had a shrine. He made an ephod and household gods, and ordained one of his sons, who became his priest. In those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did what they thought was right.

A Levite becomes Micah’s priest

There was a young man from Bethlehem in Judah, of the clan of Judah. He was a Levite and had been living there as an outsider. The man left the town of Bethlehem in Judah to find somewhere else to live. As he traveled, he came to the hill country of Ephraim, to Micah’s house. Micah asked him, “Where have you come from?” He answered, “I am a Levite from Bethlehem in Judah, and I am going to settle wherever I can find a place.” Then Micah said to him, “Stay with me, and be a father and a priest to me. I will give you about 4 ounces of silver a year, a set of clothes, and your food.” So the Levite went in. The Levite agreed to stay with the man, and the young man became like one of his own sons to him. So Micah ordained the Levite. The young man became his priest, living in Micah’s household. Then Micah said, “Now I know that the LORD will treat me well, because I have a Levite as my priest.”

fields.title: Judges 18
fields.body_html:
The Danites look for land

In those days there was no king in Israel. In those days, too, the tribe of Dan was looking for territory of its own to settle in, because until then no inheritance had fallen to it among the tribes of Israel.

So the Danites sent five capable men from their clan, chosen from their whole number, from Zorah and Eshtaol, to spy out and explore the land. They told them, “Go and explore the land.” The men came into the hill country of Ephraim as far as Micah’s house, and they stayed the night there. Near Micah’s house they recognized the young Levite’s voice, so they turned aside there. “Who brought you here?” they asked him. “What are you doing in this place? What is your business here?” He told them, “This is what Micah has done for me: he hired me, and I have become his priest.” They said to him, “Please inquire of God, so that we may know whether this journey we are on will succeed.” The priest answered them, “Go in peace. The journey you are making is under the eye of the LORD.”

The Danites take Laish

So the five men went on and came to Laish. They saw that the people there were living in security, in the way of the Sidonians, quiet and unsuspecting. No one in the land held power over them or did them harm in any way. They lived far from the Sidonians and had no dealings with anyone. When they came back to their kinsmen at Zorah and Eshtaol, their kinsmen asked them, “What news do you bring?” They answered, “Come on, let us go up against them! We have seen the land, and it is very good. And here you sit doing nothing! Do not be slow to go in and take possession of the land. When you go, you will come to an unsuspecting people and a spacious land. God has given it into your hands, a place that lacks nothing on earth.” So 600 men of the clan of the Danites, armed with weapons of war, set out from there, from Zorah and Eshtaol. They went up and made camp at Kiriath-jearim in Judah. This is why the place west of Kiriath-jearim has been called Mahaneh-dan to this day. From there they went on into the hill country of Ephraim and came to Micah’s house. Then the five men who had spied out the land of Laish said to their kinsmen, “Did you know that in these houses there is an ephod, household gods, a carved image and a cast idol? Now think about what you should do.” So they turned aside there, came to the young Levite’s house at Micah’s place, and greeted him. Meanwhile the 600 armed men of Dan stood at the entrance of the gate. The five men who had spied out the land went up, entered the house, and took the carved image, the ephod, the household gods and the cast idol, while the priest was standing at the gate’s entrance with the 600 armed men. When these men went into Micah’s house and took the carved image, the ephod, the household gods and the cast idol, the priest said to them, “What are you doing?” They answered him, “Be quiet! Put your hand over your mouth and come with us. Be a father and a priest to us. Which is better: to be priest for one man’s household, or for a tribe and clan in Israel?” The priest was pleased. He took the ephod, the household gods and the carved image, and went along among the people. They turned and set off, putting their children, their livestock and their goods in front of them. When they had gone some distance from Micah’s house, the men who lived in the houses near Micah’s were called out, and they caught up with the Danites. As they shouted after the Danites, the Danites turned around. “What is the matter with you,” they said to Micah, “that you have called out these men?” He answered, “You have taken the gods I made, and the priest, and gone off. What do I have left? How can you ask me, ‘What is the matter with you?’” The Danites told him, “Do not raise your voice at us, or some hot-tempered men may attack you, and you will lose your life and the lives of your household.” So the Danites went on their way. Micah saw that they were too strong for him, so he turned around and went back home. So they took what Micah had made, along with the priest who had been his, and came to Laish, to a quiet and unsuspecting people. They struck them down with the sword and burned the city. There was no one to rescue them, because the city was far from Sidon and they had no dealings with anyone. It lay in the valley that belongs to Beth-rehob. The Danites rebuilt the city and settled there. They named the city Dan, after their ancestor Dan, who was born to Israel; but the city used to be called Laish. The Danites set up the carved image for themselves. Jonathan son of Gershom, son of Manasseh, and his sons served as priests for the tribe of Dan until the time the land went into exile. They kept Micah’s carved image, which he had made, set up for themselves the whole time the house of God was at Shiloh.

fields.title: Judges 19
fields.body_html:
A Levite, his concubine and the men of Gibeah

In those days, when there was no king in Israel, a Levite was living for a time in the far reaches of the hill country of Ephraim. He took a concubine for himself from Bethlehem in Judah. But his concubine was unfaithful to him. She left him and went back to her father’s house in Bethlehem in Judah, and she stayed there for some time, four months. Her husband set out after her to speak tenderly to her and win her back. He took his servant and two donkeys with him. She brought him into her father’s house, and when the young woman’s father saw him, he was glad to meet him. His father-in-law, the young woman’s father, pressed him to stay, so he remained with him three days. They ate and drank and spent the nights there. They rose early on the morning of the fourth day, and he made ready to leave. But the young woman’s father said to his son-in-law, “Have a bite to eat first to strengthen yourself; then you can go.” So the two of them sat down and ate and drank together. Then the young woman’s father said to the man, “Please agree to stay the night and enjoy yourself.” When the man got up to go, his father-in-law kept urging him, so he stayed there another night. He rose early on the morning of the fifth day to leave, but the young woman’s father said, “Strengthen yourself with some food first, and stay until the afternoon.” So the two of them ate together. When the man got up to go, with his concubine and his servant, his father-in-law, the young woman’s father, said to him, “Look, the day is fading into evening. Please stay the night. The day is nearly over; spend the night here and enjoy yourself. Tomorrow you can get up early and be on your way home.” But the man refused to stay the night. He got up and set out, and came as far as the place facing Jebus, that is, Jerusalem. He had with him two saddled donkeys, and his concubine was with him. They were close to Jebus, and the day was nearly over, when the servant said to his master, “Come, let us stop at this Jebusite city and spend the night there.” His master answered, “We will not stop in a city of foreigners, where none of the people are Israelites. We will go on to Gibeah.” He said to his servant, “Come, let us try to reach one of these places and spend the night in Gibeah or Ramah.” So they passed on and went their way, and the sun set as they came near Gibeah of Benjamin. They turned off the road there to go in and spend the night at Gibeah. He went in and sat down in the town square, but no one took them into a home for the night. Then, that evening, an old man came in from his work in the fields. He was from the hill country of Ephraim and was living in Gibeah as an outsider; the men of the town were Benjamites. When he looked up and saw the traveler in the town square, the old man asked, “Where are you going? Where have you come from?” He answered, “We are traveling from Bethlehem in Judah to the far reaches of the hill country of Ephraim. That is my home. I had gone to Bethlehem in Judah, and I am on my way to the house of the LORD. But nobody here will take me into his home. We have straw and feed of our own for the donkeys, and bread and wine for me, for your servant woman, and for the young man with your servants. We are not short of anything.” The old man said, “You are welcome. Leave all your needs to me. Just do not spend the night in the square.” So he brought him into his house and fed the donkeys. They washed their feet, and they ate and drank. While they were enjoying themselves, the men of the city, worthless men, surrounded the house and kept pounding on the door. They called to the old man, the owner of the house, “Bring out the man who has come into your house, so we can have sex with him.” The owner of the house went out to them and said, “No, my brothers, please do not do such evil. This man has come into my house as my guest. Do not do this disgraceful thing. Here is my daughter, a virgin, and his concubine. Let me bring them out to you. Violate them and do with them whatever you like. But do not do this disgraceful thing to this man.” But the men refused to listen to him. So the Levite took hold of his concubine and put her out to them. They raped her and abused her all night until morning, and let her go as dawn was breaking. At daybreak the woman came and collapsed at the door of the man’s house where her master was, and lay there until it was light. Her master got up in the morning, opened the doors of the house, and went out to continue his journey. And there was the woman, his concubine, lying collapsed in the doorway of the house, her hands on the threshold. He said to her, “Get up; let us go.” But there was no answer. Then he put her on the donkey, and the man set out and went home. When he reached his house, he took a knife, took hold of his concubine, and cut her up limb by limb into twelve pieces. Then he sent the pieces throughout all the territory of Israel. Everyone who saw it said, “Nothing like this has ever happened or been seen, from the day the Israelites came up out of Egypt until now. Think about it! Take counsel and speak up!”

fields.title: Judges 20
fields.body_html:
The tribes gather at Mizpah

Then all the Israelites came out, from Dan to Beersheba and from the land of Gilead, and the congregation gathered as one before the LORD at Mizpah. The leaders of the whole people, of all the tribes of Israel, took their places in the assembly of the people of God: 400,000 foot soldiers armed with swords.

The Benjaminites heard that the Israelites had gone up to Mizpah. Then the Israelites said, “Tell us how this evil thing happened.” The Levite, the husband of the murdered woman, answered, “My concubine and I came to Gibeah in Benjamin to spend the night. The men of Gibeah rose against me and surrounded the house at night to get me. They meant to kill me. They raped my concubine, and she died. So I took my concubine, cut her into pieces, and sent them throughout the whole land Israel had inherited, because they had done a shameful and outrageous thing in Israel. Now all of you, the Israelites, give your advice and decide what to do here.” All the people rose up as one and said, “None of us will go home to his tent. Not one of us will return to his house. This is what we will do to Gibeah: we will go up against it as the lot decides. We will take ten men out of every 100 from all the tribes of Israel, 100 out of every 1,000, and 1,000 out of every 10,000, to bring food for the army. Then, when the army comes to Gibeah in Benjamin, it can repay them for all the outrage they committed in Israel.” So all the men of Israel gathered against the city, united as one.

Benjamin refuses to hand over the men of Gibeah

The tribes of Israel sent men through the whole tribe of Benjamin to say, “What is this evil thing that has been done among you? Now hand over those worthless men in Gibeah, so that we can put them to death and remove this evil from Israel.” But the Benjaminites would not listen to their brothers, the Israelites. Instead the Benjaminites came together from their towns to Gibeah, to go out and fight against the Israelites. That day the Benjaminites called up from their towns 26,000 men armed with swords, besides the people of Gibeah, who called up 700 chosen men. Among all these soldiers were 700 picked men who fought left-handed, each able to sling a stone at a hair without missing.

The men of Israel, not counting Benjamin, called up 400,000 men armed with swords, all of them experienced fighters. The Israelites set out and went up to Bethel, and they asked God, “Which of us should go up first to fight against the Benjaminites?” The LORD answered, “Judah is to go first.” The next morning the Israelites set out and camped facing Gibeah.

War against Benjamin

The men of Israel went out to fight Benjamin and drew up their battle lines against them at Gibeah. Then the Benjaminites came out of Gibeah and cut down 22,000 men of Israel on the battlefield that day. But the army, the men of Israel, took courage and again drew up their battle lines in the same place where they had drawn them up on the first day. The Israelites went up and wept before the LORD until evening, and they asked the LORD, “Should we again go into battle against our brothers the Benjaminites?” The LORD answered, “Go up against them.”

So the Israelites advanced against the Benjaminites on the second day. Benjamin came out of Gibeah to meet them on the second day and again cut down 18,000 of the Israelites on the battlefield, all of them armed with swords. Then all the Israelites, the whole army, went up to Bethel. They sat there weeping before the LORD, and they fasted that day until evening and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before the LORD. And the Israelites asked the LORD. The ark of the covenant of God was kept there in those days, and Phinehas son of Eleazar, son of Aaron, served before it. They asked, “Should we go out again to fight against our brothers the Benjaminites, or should we stop?” The LORD answered, “Go up, for tomorrow I will hand them over to you.” So Israel set men in ambush all around Gibeah.

On the third day the Israelites went up against the Benjaminites and drew up their battle lines against Gibeah as they had done before. The Benjaminites came out to meet the army and were drawn away from the town. As before, they began to strike down some of the troops on the roads, one leading up to Bethel and the other to Gibeah, in the open country. They killed about thirty men of Israel. The Benjaminites said, “They are being beaten by us as they were before.” But the Israelites had said, “Let us run away and draw them out from the town onto the roads.” All the men of Israel rose up from where they were and drew up their battle lines at Baal-tamar, while the men of Israel in ambush burst out from their position west of Geba. Then 10,000 chosen men from all Israel came against Gibeah, and the fighting was fierce. The Benjaminites did not realize that disaster was about to strike them.

Benjamin is defeated

The LORD defeated Benjamin before Israel, and that day the Israelites cut down 25,100 men of Benjamin, all of them armed with swords. Then the Benjaminites saw that they were beaten. The men of Israel had given ground to Benjamin, because they were counting on the ambush they had set against Gibeah. The men in ambush moved quickly and rushed into Gibeah. They spread out and struck down the whole town with the sword. The men of Israel had agreed on a signal with the men in ambush: they were to send up a great cloud of smoke from the town. Then the men of Israel turned around in the battle. Benjamin had already started cutting down the men of Israel and had killed about thirty of them, and they said, “They are surely beaten by us, as in the first battle.” But when the signal began to rise from the town in a column of smoke, the Benjaminites looked behind them, and there was the whole town going up in smoke to the sky. Then the men of Israel turned to fight, and the men of Benjamin were terrified, because they saw that disaster had come upon them. So they turned and fled from the men of Israel toward the wilderness, but they could not escape the fighting, and those who came out of the towns cut them down in the middle of it. They surrounded the Benjaminites and chased them, and they trampled them down at Menuhah, as far as the area east of Gibeah. Of Benjamin 18,000 men fell, all of them brave warriors. Then they turned and ran toward the wilderness, to the rock of Rimmon. The Israelites picked off 5,000 men along the roads, and they kept after them as far as Gidom and killed 2,000 more. So in all 25,000 men of Benjamin who were armed with swords fell that day, all of them brave warriors. But 600 men turned and escaped into the wilderness to the rock of Rimmon, and they stayed there four months. Then the men of Israel turned back against the Benjaminites and struck them down with the sword, from the people of the towns to the animals, everything they found. They also set on fire every town they came to.

fields.title: Judges 21
fields.body_html:
The tribes grieve for Benjamin

Now the men of Israel had taken an oath at Mizpah: “None of us will give his daughter in marriage to a man of Benjamin.” The people went to Bethel and sat there before God until evening, weeping aloud and bitterly. “The LORD, God of Israel,” they cried, “why has this happened in Israel? Why should Israel be missing one of its tribes today?” Early the next morning the people built an altar there and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings.

Wives from Jabesh-gilead

Then the Israelites asked, “Is there anyone from all the tribes of Israel who did not come up with the assembly to the LORD?” For they had bound themselves by a solemn oath: whoever stayed away from the LORD at Mizpah must be put to death. But the Israelites grieved for their brother tribe Benjamin. “Today,” they said, “one tribe has been cut off from Israel. How can we provide wives for the men who are left, since we have sworn by the LORD not to give them any of our daughters in marriage?” So they asked, “Who from the tribes of Israel did not come up to the LORD at Mizpah?” It turned out that not a single man from Jabesh-gilead had come into the camp to join the assembly. When the people were counted, not one of those who lived in Jabesh-gilead was there. So the congregation sent 12,000 of its best fighting men there with these orders: “Go and put the people of Jabesh-gilead to the sword, the women and children too. Here is what you must do: every male, and every woman who has slept with a man, you are to devote to destruction.” Among the people of Jabesh-gilead they found 400 young women who were virgins and had never slept with a man. These they brought to the camp at Shiloh, in the land of Canaan.

Then the whole congregation sent word to the Benjaminites at the rock of Rimmon and offered them peace. So Benjamin came back at that time, and they were given the women of Jabesh-gilead whom the Israelites had spared. But there were not enough for them all. The people grieved for Benjamin, because the LORD had torn a gap in the tribes of Israel. Then the elders of the congregation said, “How can we provide wives for the men who are left, since the women of Benjamin have been wiped out?” They said, “The survivors of Benjamin must have heirs to keep their inheritance, so that a tribe is not wiped out of Israel. Yet we cannot give them our daughters as wives, because the Israelites have sworn, ‘A curse on anyone who gives a wife to Benjamin!’”

The dance at Shiloh

Then they said, “Look, every year there is a festival of the LORD at Shiloh.” (Shiloh lies north of Bethel and south of Lebonah, east of the highway that runs up from Bethel to Shechem.) So they instructed the Benjaminites, “Go and hide in the vineyards and wait, and watch. When the young women of Shiloh come out to join in the dances, rush out of the vineyards, and each of you seize a wife for himself from the young women of Shiloh. Then go back to the land of Benjamin. When their fathers or brothers come to us to protest, we will tell them, ‘Do us a kindness and let them keep the women, because we did not take a wife for each of them in the war. And since you did not give them your daughters, you are not guilty of breaking the oath.’”

The Benjaminites did just that. They carried off as many wives as there were men, from the dancers they had seized, and went back to their own land. They rebuilt their towns and settled in them. At that time the Israelites left that place and went home, each man to his own tribe and clan, each to his own land. In those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did what they thought was right.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
In those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did what they thought was right.

— Judges 21:25

Judges ends with the same words it has been repeating for five chapters. There is no final victory, no last judge, no word of comfort from the narrator. The tribes go home, “each man to his own tribe and clan”, from a war in which they nearly destroyed one of their own. And the book closes on a diagnosis.

The question the book leaves with you

The diagnosis has two halves, and both matter. “There was no king in Israel”: the people needed someone to lead them, to hold them together, to keep them faithful to the covenant. And “everyone did what they thought was right”: the deeper trouble was not the lack of a government but the human heart left to itself.

That is the question Judges leaves with every reader: what will it take to rescue people who keep needing to be rescued? Again and again God raised up a deliverer, and again and again the rescue lasted only as long as the deliverer lived. Gideon refused a crown and then made an idol. Samson only began to save Israel. Every judge died, and every death began the slide again. The book has shown, with painful honesty, that a better leader is necessary. It has also shown that a better leader would not be enough, unless he could change the heart.

Where the story goes next

The next book in the English Bible, Ruth, opens “In the days when the judges judged”, and shows a different side of the same dark time: an ordinary family in Bethlehem, a Moabite widow who chose Israel’s God, and a man who kept the law with kindness. It ends with the name of David. Then 1 Samuel begins with a woman praying in the sanctuary at Shiloh, and her son becomes the last of the judges and anoints the first two kings. The refrain of Judges is answered: there will be a king in Israel. And the book of Samuel will show that kings, too, can do what they think is right.

The New Testament gathers the judges into its long list of faith. “Time would run out on me,” says the letter to the Hebrews, “if I told about Gideon, Barak, Samson and Jephthah”, people who, for all their failures, “found strength when they were weak”. And the Christian church has always read the pattern of Judges as a promise. The deliverers came with the Spirit of the LORD on them, and saved, and died. The gospel announces a Deliverer on whom the Spirit rested without measure, who saved by his death, and who did not stay dead. He is the King Judges was waiting for, and he does more than rule: he gives a new heart.

Where to go from here

Judges has been read in the church as a mirror of the Christian life, its failures and its rescues, and some of the best of that reading is in this library. A few places to begin:

  • On the whole book. Hannah Whitall Smith’s Old Testament Types and Teachings, whose chapter “Judges: The Christian’s Failures” reads the book as a warning of the failures that beset believers; and A. B. Simpson’s The Holy Spirit, or Power from on High, whose chapter “The Holy Spirit in the Book of Judges” follows the Spirit from Othniel to Samson.
  • On the cycle (Judges 2). Two sermons by A. B. Simpson: Bochim, or the Cause of Spiritual Failure (Judges 2:5) and Sinning and Repenting (Judges 2:14–19).
  • On Gideon (Judges 6–7). Simpson’s Gideon, or the Strength of Weakness, on the call of Gideon and the three hundred, and his The Weapons of Our Warfare, on the torches, jars and horns of Judges 7.
  • On Jephthah (Judges 11). Simpson’s Jephthah, or the Faith That Leads to Faithfulness (Judges 11:30–36).
  • On Samson (Judges 13–16). E. M. Bounds’s Prayer and Praying Men, whose chapter “Praying Saints of the Old Testaments” dwells on Samson’s last prayer.
  • On the judges and faith. The closing chapter, “What More Shall I Say?”, of Gareth Evans’s He Holds My Tomorrows, on Hebrews 11:32–40 and the judges it names.
  • For reading with children. “Deborah and the Rainstorm”, “Gideon’s Small Army” and “Samson the Strong” in Tell Me the Story – Book 2: Out of Egypt, and “Everyone Did What Was Right in Their Own Eyes”, on Judges 2 and Ruth, in The Big Story, both Ochorus Originals.

You can also go the other way, from the text to the classics. Every reference to Judges in this library can be tapped to read the verse, and the Scripture pages gather, chapter by chapter, what the great writers of the church have said about each passage of this book.

And then read on, into Ruth and Samuel, where the darkness of Judges begins to give way to a promise. But first let the book’s one tender sentence stay with you. In the middle of all Israel’s faithlessness, when they had put away their foreign gods at last and turned back to him, this is what it says of God:

Then they got rid of the foreign gods that were among them and served the LORD, and he could bear Israel’s misery no longer.

— Judges 10:16
